title: 20 EMA Pullback
teaches: The 20 EMA pullback as we trade it: a leader in a rising trend, above its 200-day with the 20 EMA over a rising 50-day, drifts quietly back to the rising 20 EMA, a session holds the line, the buy is a cent over that session's high at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under its low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: the odds are very high that when a security makes a new momentum high and pulls back, it will retest its recent high. Therefore, any pullback from a new momentum high can be bought.
facts.claim: Raschke on the Holy Grail: after a new momentum high the odds are very high a pullback retests the recent high, so any such pullback can be bought.

facts.quote: 2. Look for a retracement in price to the 20 period exponential moving average. This will usually be accompanied by a turndown in the ADX.
facts.claim: Raschke's rule: look for a retracement to the 20-period exponential moving average.

facts.quote: 3. When the price touches the 20 period moving average, put a buy stop above the high of the previous bar.
facts.claim: Raschke's buy: a buy stop above the high of the previous bar once price touches the 20-period average.

facts.quote: 4. Once filled, enter a protective sell stop at the newly formed swing low. Trail stops as profits grow.
facts.claim: Raschke's stop: the newly formed swing low, trailed as profits grow.

facts.quote: This is a case where there is no reason to be in this trade.
facts.claim: Raschke on a pullback buy that showed little movement for five days: no reason to be in the trade.

facts.quote: On the 30-minute time frame, the ADX rose above 30, so we’ll buy the first retrace-ment to the 20-period EMA and look to exit on a push to new highs.
facts.claim: Raschke buys the first retracement to the 20-period EMA after a strong trend.

facts.quote: I use market orders most of the time.
facts.claim: Raschke uses market orders most of the time.

facts.quote: By focusing on the 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages (EMAs), you can identify key moments to buy stocks when the price dips into these levels after a strong rally.
facts.claim: Kell: buy the dip into the 10 and 20-day EMAs after a strong rally.

facts.quote: But always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in before making your trade.
facts.claim: Kell: always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback refers to the first time the stock price retests its moving averages after a strong upward move, called a “Wedge Pop.”
facts.claim: Kell: the EMA Crossback is the first retest of the averages after a Wedge Pop.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback works best when the price gently moves sideways, allowing the moving averages to rise to the price.
facts.claim: Kell: the pullback works best when price drifts sideways and the rising averages catch up.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price “surfs” the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a leader surfs its rising 10 and 20-day lines and sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day, no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi wants a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months first.

facts.quote: If a beginner stick to the 10-day. You wait for the first CLOSE below the 10- day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails the 10-day and sells on the first close below it.

facts.quote: As long as the price remains above the 21-day EMA, any short-term movements can be considered noise, rather than a clear signal of a change in trend.
facts.claim: Keller: above the 21-day EMA, short-term moves are noise, not a change of trend.

facts.quote: The price is above the 21-day EMA, the 21-day is above the 50-day SMA, and the 50-day is above the 200-day SMA.
facts.claim: Keller's proper order: price over the 21-day EMA, over the 50-day, over the 200-day.

facts.quote: I think of the 21-day EMA as the first line of defense, an initial stop within an uptrend phase.
facts.claim: Keller calls the 21-day EMA the first line of defense in an uptrend.

facts.quote: chasing stocks hitting a new high in price can be the surest way to frustration
facts.claim: McGonagle: chasing new highs is the surest way to frustration; wait for the pullback.

facts.quote: While you can use either the shorter-term 10-day or the longer-term 21-day moving average, you’ll want to check the stock’s chart to uncover which one is the better indicator.
facts.claim: McGonagle: check which line, the 10-day or the 21-day, the stock itself obeys.

facts.quote: a moving average gives you a reason to study price action closely as it approaches, not a reason to act automatically.
facts.claim: Shannon: a moving average is a reason to watch price closely, not a reason to act automatically.

facts.quote: Brian looks for volume expanding in the direction of the primary trend and contracting during pullbacks.
facts.claim: Shannon looks for volume contracting during pullbacks.

facts.quote: The official trade ideas typically use suggested stops 2 to 3% from the entry price
facts.claim: Shannon's trade ideas use stops 2 to 3% from the entry.

facts.quote: When price is above a longer-term reference, such as the 200-day moving average, the larger trend is considered innocent until proven guilty.
facts.claim: AlphaTrends: above the 200-day the larger trend is innocent until proven guilty.

facts.quote: Buying strength after a controlled pullback is very different from chasing price after an extended rally.
facts.claim: AlphaTrends: buying strength after a controlled pullback is not chasing an extended rally.

facts.quote: In most small caps there is one big rally and then they exhaust themselves. Buying such pullbacks on most of them would make you a bag holder.
facts.claim: Bonde: buying pullbacks in most small caps makes you a bag holder.

facts.quote: Buy first pullback after a major breakout.
facts.claim: Bonde lists buying the first pullback after a major breakout as a common pullback method.

facts.quote: A slow drift into the EMAs is ideal.
facts.claim: TraderLion: a slow drift into the EMAs is the ideal pullback.

facts.quote: Place your stop-loss just below the most recent swing low or consolidation base.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the stop goes just below the most recent swing low.

facts.quote: A 20-period EMA applies a 9.52% weighting to the most recent price (2/(20+1) = .0952).
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a 20-period EMA weights the latest price 9.52%.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

facts.claim: D40: growing sales and earnings preferred; the chart comes first.

facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.claim: The touch: the hold session's low within 0.25 ATR above to 1 ATR below the 20 EMA.

facts.claim: The pullback is at least 1 ATR off the swing high, measured from the highest high of the last 11 sessions to the hold session's low.

facts.claim: The pullback lasts 2 to 15 sessions from the swing high to the hold session.

walkthroughs.title: GE, January 2024: the low kisses the line
steps: GE, January 2024. A leader in a rising trend drifts four days back to its rising 20 EMA on 0.78x volume.
The hold session: the low kisses the line to the cent and closes above it. Above the 50-day and 200-day.
Next session trades a cent over the hold candle's high. Buy at market, 100.39. Stop a few cents under its low, 99.07.
Failure mode: a slice back through the line that takes the day's low. Instead, 3R in 5 sessions. A third comes off.

walkthroughs.title: NVDA, May 2023: the textbook leader, out before the report
steps: NVDA, May 2023. A rising line, a light-volume four-day rest, 1.4 ATR off the high, pullback volume 0.74x.
The hold session closes above the line. Buy a cent over its high at market, 28.79. Stop under its low, 28.02.
3R in 3 sessions: a third off, stop to breakeven. It stood at 3.9R the day before the report.
Hold through a report only if up 5R. We are out before the gap. The rule costs one gap and saves many.

walkthroughs.title: CRM, June 2020: the shallow shakeout
steps: CRM, June 2020. A four-day pullback, 2.4 ATR off the high on 0.76x volume. The low dips 0.28 ATR under the line.
The same session closes back above the 20 EMA. That is a shakeout, not a lost line. The hold is in.
Next session trades a cent over the hold candle's high. Buy at market, 183.72. Stop a few cents under its low, 179.97.
Failure mode: a second close under the line before the trigger. Instead, 3R in 2 sessions. A third off, stop to breakeven.

questions.q: In one line, what is a 20 EMA pullback?
choices: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA
A stock sliding below a falling 20 EMA
A tight box under a flat ceiling
A sharp V-bottom off the 200-day
questions.answer: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA
questions.why: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA. Our pattern is a quiet pullback of 2 to 15 sessions. It is at least 1 ATR deep and ends at a rising 20 EMA. Kullamagi: a leader surfs its rising 10 and 20-day lines. Raschke: look for a retracement to the 20-period EMA.
questions.lesson_line: A pullback is a leader catching its breath at a line that is still rising.

wrong.A tight box under a flat ceiling: That is a flat base. A pullback is a dip to a moving line, not a rest under a level.
wrong.A sharp V-bottom off the 200-day: A pullback sits in a rising trend above the 200-day. A V-bottom is a reversal.
wrong.A stock sliding below a falling 20 EMA: That is a downtrend. A pullback needs a leader and a 20 EMA that is still rising.

questions.simple: It is a strong stock taking a short, quiet rest at a 20 EMA line that is still rising.

deeper.example: GE, January 2024: four days back to its 20 EMA on 0.78x volume. The low kissed the line to the cent. That is the shape of the setup.

reasons: card numbers are proposed, not rulings
several facts agree

questions.q: Which line must the hold session close above, by our hard rule?
choices: The 200-day simple average
The 50-day SMA, if it is rising
The 9 EMA, closing back over it
No line; the touch is enough
questions.why: The 200-day simple moving average. The card has the hold session close above it, and we take no longs below it, unless it is a parabolic long. AlphaTrends: above the 200-day the larger trend is innocent until proven guilty. The 50-day and the 9 EMA are not the hard line.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there is no pullback to buy, only a bounce.

wrong.The 50-day SMA, if it is rising: The 50-day is part of the context, not the hard line. The hard line is the 200-day.
wrong.The 9 EMA, closing back over it: The 9 EMA is a confirming sign in grading, not a gate.
wrong.No line; the touch is enough: The touch is the pattern. The 200-day is the context that must be there first.

questions.simple: The 200-day line, because we do not buy stocks that sit below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B26

questions.q: On a 20 EMA pullback the stop goes a few cents under the low of the session that held the line.
questions.why: True. The stop goes a few cents under the low of the session that held the line, not exactly on it. Stop first, then the size from it. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Kullamagi also sets the stop at the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the hold session's low.
questions.simple: True, because the stop goes just under the low of the session that held the line, never exactly on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The 20 EMA must be ___: higher than it was 10 sessions earlier.
questions.why: Rising. The 20 EMA must be higher than it was 10 sessions earlier. A line that flattens or turns down before entry ends the setup. Kell: the pullback works best when the rising averages catch up to the price.
questions.lesson_line: A rising line is the whole setup. A flat one is a different chart.
questions.simple: The line must be higher than it was 10 sessions ago, so the stock rests on a line that still climbs.

reasons: the 10-session test is a proposed card number

questions.q: A session held the 20 EMA and closed above it. Where is the buy we draw on the chart?
choices: A cent over the hold candle's high
At the close of the hold session
A limit order resting on the 20 EMA
A close back over the 9 EMA
questions.answer: A cent over the hold candle's high
questions.why: A cent over the hold candle's high, bought at market on a later session. The close is not the trigger. A limit order on the line buys before anything has held. The 9 EMA remount is only a confirming sign. Raschke: a buy stop above the high of the previous bar once price touches the line.
questions.lesson_line: The hold candle sets the trigger. Over its high, we are in.

wrong.At the close of the hold session: The close is the hold itself, not the buy. Our buy waits for price to trade over the hold candle's high on a later session.
wrong.A limit order resting on the 20 EMA: That buys before anything has held. Never buy before a session holds the line.
wrong.A close back over the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA remount is a confirming sign in grading, not the trigger.

questions.simple: We buy at market once price trades a cent over the high of the session that held the line.

deeper.trap: Buying the touch itself, before any session has held, is a named mistake. Kell: always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in. The hold candle's high is a level to set an alert on, and the buy happens only when it trades.

reasons: the cent-over-the-high buy is the proposed fallback trigger, held under D-003

questions.q: Entries on a 20 EMA pullback are limit orders placed on the 20 EMA, in regular hours only.
questions.why: False. Entries are market orders, not limit orders resting on the 20 EMA. We buy in regular trading hours only, with no new buys outside them. Raschke is one voice on this: I use market orders most of the time.
questions.lesson_line: Market order the moment it trades. Regular hours only.
questions.simple: False, because we enter with market orders in regular hours, not limit orders resting on the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E57 and E58

questions.q: If the trend is strong enough, you may buy the first touch of the 20 EMA before any session has held it.
questions.why: False. Never buy before a session actually holds the line, however strong the trend. Kell: always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in. Shannon: a moving average is a reason to watch price closely, not a reason to act automatically.
questions.lesson_line: The line is a place to watch, not a reason to act. Let a session hold it first.
questions.simple: False, because the line is only a place to watch, so we wait for a session to hold it first.

reasons: the never-before-hold rule is a proposed card line
if D-003 moves the buy to the hold session itself, the wording may need a re-read

questions.q: During the pullback the session's low reaches under the 50-day SMA. Which card is it now, if anything?
choices: The 50-day MA pullback
Still the 20 EMA pullback
A Remount of the 50-day
A bull flag on the 50-day
questions.why: The 50-day form of the moving-average pullback, if anything. The 20 EMA pullback needs the hold session's low to stay above the 50-day SMA. Once the low reaches the 50-day, the 50-day is the line, and it is judged on its own card.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line the low touched. The 50-day is a different card.

wrong.Still the 20 EMA pullback: The 20 EMA pullback's low holds above the 50-day. This low went through it.
wrong.A Remount of the 50-day: A Remount is a line lost and retaken, not a dip. One session's low under the 50-day is not that.
wrong.A bull flag on the 50-day: A flag needs a pole. The question here is only which line the low touched.

questions.simple: The 50-day pullback, because the low went down to the 50-day, so that is the line that was tested.

reasons: the 50-day boundary is a proposed card line
fixed before

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card, the pullback lasts 2 to ___ sessions from the swing high to the hold session.
questions.why: 15. The card says the pullback lasts 2 to 15 sessions from the swing high to the hold session. Our examples ran 4 to 10 sessions, such as TOL's 10-day drift. A drift past 15 sessions does not fit this card.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions: two to fifteen on our card.
questions.simple: On our card a pullback may last at most 15 sessions, counted from the swing high to the hold session.

deeper.example: TOL in 2004 drifted 10 days down to the line on 0.69x volume and reached 3R in 6 sessions. GE took only 4 days. Both fit the 2 to 15 session window, so the cap is a limit, not a target.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c04)
the 2 to 15 length is a proposed number that may change; other dossiers say 2 to 8 and 2 to 10
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which pullback into the 20 EMA is orderly by our card?
choices: Small red days on quiet volume
One huge red day to the line
A red day on heavy volume
A gap down past the 50-day
questions.answer: Small red days on quiet volume
questions.why: Small red days on quiet volume. Orderly means no down day larger than 2 ATR and none on more than 1.5 times the 50-day average volume. Shannon: volume contracts during pullbacks. TraderLion: a slow drift into the EMAs is ideal.
questions.lesson_line: Orderly means small bars and quiet volume. A big red day is selling, not resting.

wrong.One huge red day to the line: Orderly allows no down day larger than 2 ATR. One huge red bar breaks that.
wrong.A red day on heavy volume: A down day on more than 1.5 times the 50-day volume is distribution, not a rest.
wrong.A gap down past the 50-day: That broke the 50-day. The 20 EMA pullback is off.

questions.simple: A quiet drift of small red days is orderly, while big or heavy-volume down days are selling.

reasons: the 2 ATR and 1.5x limits are proposed card numbers

questions.q: A stock drifting along its 20 EMA, no swing high at least 1 ATR above the hold low, has not pulled back.
questions.why: True. The card needs the pullback to be at least 1 ATR off the swing high. That is measured from the highest high of the last 11 sessions to the hold session's low. A stock sliding along the line with no such dip has nothing to pull back from.
questions.lesson_line: You need something to pull back from. Measure the dip in ATR.
questions.simple: True, because the card needs a dip of at least 1 ATR from the swing high before it counts as a pullback.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c03)
the 1 ATR depth and the 11 session window are proposed numbers
tied to held decision D-029
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which low counts as a touch by the card?
choices: Low of 51.00
A low of 48.30
Low of 47.90
Low of 46.00
questions.why: A low of 48.30. The touch band runs from 0.25 ATR above the 20 EMA to 1 ATR below it. With an ATR of 2.00, 48.30 is under the line by less than one ATR. The line gets run through; it is not a wall.
questions.lesson_line: A touch has a band: a little above the line, up to one ATR under it.

wrong.Low of 51.00: That low stayed more than 0.25 ATR above the line. It never came down to touch it.
wrong.Low of 47.90: That is under the line by more than one ATR of 2.00. It went through the touch band, not into it.
wrong.Low of 46.00: That is far more than one ATR under the line. The line gets run through, but not by that much.

questions.story: Four stocks each have a 20 EMA at 50.00 and an ATR of 2.00. Each closes above the line today, but their lows differ.
questions.simple: A low of 48.30, because it is under the line by less than one ATR, which is inside the touch band.

reasons: the touch band is a proposed card number
key rests on a comparison

questions.q: Two closes in a row under the 20 EMA during the pullback end the setup until it sets up again.
questions.why: True. Two closes in a row under the 20 EMA end the setup. So does a single close more than 0.5 ATR under it. One shakeout close of 0.5 ATR or less, reclaimed the next session, is still allowed. No trade until it sets up again.
questions.lesson_line: One shakeout is allowed. Two closes under the line is a line lost.
questions.simple: True, because two closes in a row under the 20 EMA end the setup until it forms again.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c14)
the two closes and 0.5 ATR lines are proposed numbers
tied to held decision D-036
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: A scanner puts the stop at the line minus 1 ATR. Why is that not our stop?
choices: Too wide; use the day's low
Too wide only for slow movers
Too tight; it sits inside the noise
Too tight; use the 50-day instead
questions.answer: Too wide; use the day's low
questions.why: Too wide. The line minus 1 ATR is wider than 1 ATR whenever the entry is above the line. Our stop is a few cents under the hold session's low, and it is a real order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is a price under a candle, not a line minus a cushion.

wrong.Too tight; it sits inside the noise: It is the other way round: a cushion under the line is wider than the day's low, not tighter.
wrong.Too wide only for slow movers: The line minus 1 ATR is wider than 1 ATR whenever the entry is above the line, for any mover.
wrong.Too tight; use the 50-day instead: The line minus 1 ATR is wider, not tighter. And our stop is not the 50-day: it is a price a few cents under the hold session's low.

questions.simple: It is too wide, because our stop goes just under the low of the hold session instead.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62

questions.q: Your initial stop can be a close under the 20 EMA that you watch for, as long as you act on it.
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. A close under a line cannot sit with the broker as an order, so it cannot be the initial stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False, because a stop must be a real order with the broker and a close under a line cannot be one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D41

questions.q: On the hold session, where does the card want the 20 EMA against the 50-day SMA?
choices: Above a rising 50-day SMA
Above a falling 50-day SMA
Below the 50-day, catching up
Crossing it that session
questions.why: Above a 50-day SMA that is itself higher than 10 sessions earlier. Keller's proper order runs price over the 21-day EMA, the 21-day over the 50-day, and the 50-day over the 200-day. Our card asks for the 20 EMA over a rising 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: Stacked and rising: the 20 EMA over a rising 50-day, with the 200-day not falling. Then look at the dip.

wrong.Below the 50-day, catching up: A 20 EMA under the 50-day is a stock in repair, not a leader resting.
wrong.Crossing it that session: A cross is the line changing sides. We want the order already settled.
wrong.Above a falling 50-day SMA: The card also wants the 50-day itself higher than it was 10 sessions earlier. A falling 50-day fails.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA should sit above a 50-day line that is climbing, which shows a healthy uptrend.

reasons: the 20-over-50 order is a proposed card line, not the owner's B26

questions.q: Is this a 20 EMA pullback?
choices: No; the line is no longer rising
No; the rise must be over 20 sessions
Yes; the touch itself is what counts
Yes, once a session holds the line
questions.answer: No; the line is no longer rising
questions.why: No. A 20 EMA that is not higher than 10 sessions earlier is no longer rising. The setup is off before any trigger. NVDA's late tap in 2025, after a four-month run, was stopped on its first day.
questions.lesson_line: A tired line does not hold. Pass the tap of a flattening 20 EMA.

wrong.No; the rise must be over 20 sessions: The card measures the rise over 10 sessions, not 20. This line is lower than it was 10 sessions ago.
wrong.Yes; the touch itself is what counts: The touch is the pattern. The rising line is the context, and it is gone.
wrong.Yes, once a session holds the line: A hold session cannot fix the context. A line that is not higher than 10 sessions earlier puts the setup off before any trigger.

questions.story: A stock has run four months. Its 20 EMA now sits lower than it was 10 sessions ago, and price drifts into it again.
questions.simple: No, because a line that has stopped rising is a tired line, so the setup is off before any buy.

reasons: the flat-line test is a proposed card number

questions.q: Buy the hold?
choices: No; the report is inside 3 days
Yes; a first tap is best
Yes; but at half size
No; it needs a second session
questions.answer: No; the report is inside 3 days
questions.why: No. We take no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, and this one reports tomorrow. The 5R exception is for holding a trade already open, not for a new buy. If the stock still sets up after the report, it can hold again.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Wait, then look again.

wrong.Yes; a first tap is best: The tap is fine, but the rulebook bars new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Yes; but at half size: Size does not change the rule. A smaller buy is still a new buy inside the window.
wrong.No; it needs a second session: One session that holds the line is enough. The reason to pass is the report inside the window.

questions.story: A leader's first tap of its rising 20 EMA holds today and closes above the line. The company reports tomorrow before the open.
questions.simple: No, because we take no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h08)
rests on the owner's rulebook B22; whether the 3 days are sessions or calendar days is held under D-072

questions.q: Bought the hold at 147.30 with the stop at 145.05. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 154.05. One R is the fill minus the stop. Three of those added to the fill give 154.05. The hard rule takes a third off there.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: The first third comes off at 154.05, which is the fill plus three times the stop distance.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h05)
computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook B19

questions.q: The last third of a 20 EMA pullback winner trails which line, by our default?
choices: The 10-day or the 21-day line
The 50-day or 200-day line
The prior day's low, daily
No trail; sell it all at 5R
questions.why: The 10-day line for a fast mover, the 21-day line for a steadier one, sold on a close below it. Kullamagi also waits for the first close below the 10-day. The last third rides this trail after the thirds at 3R and 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.

wrong.The 50-day or 200-day line: Our default trail is the 10-day or the 21-day line, not these.
wrong.The prior day's low, daily: Our default trails an average and sells on a close below it, not a daily low.
wrong.No trail; sell it all at 5R: 5R is where the second third comes off, not the exit. The last third rides the trail.

questions.simple: We trail the 10-day line for fast movers or the 21-day line for steadier ones, and sell on a close below it.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h21)
rests on the owner's rulebook E52; trail timing is held under D-024
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: We buy this pullback in leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.why: True. Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. The only exceptions are parabolic and mean-reversion trades. Bonde: buying pullbacks in most small caps would make you a bag holder.
questions.lesson_line: A pullback in a laggard is a dip in a downtrend. Buy the leaders.
questions.simple: True, because we only buy leaders with a strong rating in a strong group, not laggards.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C31
Bonde's quote is about small caps

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A down day into the line on more than ___ times the 50-day average volume is distribution, not a pullback.
questions.why: 1.5. A down day into the line on more than 1.5 times the 50-day average volume is distribution, not a pullback. The setup is off before any trigger. Shannon looks for volume contracting during pullbacks.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet into the line is a rest. Loud into the line is selling.
questions.simple: It is 1.5 times the 50-day average volume, and a red day above that is heavy selling, not a rest.

reasons: the 1.5x limit is a proposed card number

questions.q: What is true of your trade now?
choices: Stopped out; the loss is booked
Still in; it closed above 59.17
Stopped out; a re-buy needs no trigger
Still in; stops only count on closes
questions.answer: Stopped out; the loss is booked
questions.why: Stopped out. The stop is the exit, and the day's low of 58.57 traded through the stop at 59.17. The later close at 59.21 does not undo that. GILD did this and went on without us. A loss at the stop is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at the stop is the system working, not a mistake.

wrong.Still in; it closed above 59.17: The stop order fired when the low traded through it. A later close above the stop does not undo that.
wrong.Stopped out; a re-buy needs no trigger: After a stop-out we buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade. A bounce is not a trigger.
wrong.Still in; stops only count on closes: A stop order fires when price trades through it. It does not wait for a close.

questions.story: You bought the hold at 60.50 with the stop at 59.17. Next day the stock trades down through the stop, the low prints 58.57, and it closes back at 59.21.
questions.simple: You were stopped out, because the low traded through the stop and a later close above it does not undo that.

deeper.example: GILD in 2013: bought at 60.50 with the stop at 59.17. Next day the low hit 58.57 and the stop fired, then it closed back at 59.21. It reached the 3R level (64.49) on 09-18 and 5R (67.15) on 10-17 without us. The loss was still the plan working.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A4 and B21
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Ten trading days after the buy the trade sits at 0.6R, doing nothing. Our rule?
choices: Sell it and free up the money
Hold; the stop will do the exiting
Add another third at a higher price
Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it and free up the money
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. At 0.6R after 10 days it has not earned its place. Raschke on a pullback buy that went nowhere: there is no reason to be in this trade.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.

wrong.Hold; the stop will do the exiting: The stop is one exit. The time stop is the other, and ten days have passed.
wrong.Add another third at a higher price: No adding, and nothing is working. The rule frees the money.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. At 0.6R the time stop applies.

questions.simple: Sell, because a trade still under 1R after 10 days is not working, so we free the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C33

questions.q: The highest high of the last 11 sessions is 120.00, ATR is 3.00 and the hold session's low is 117.60. How deep is the pullback, in ATR?
questions.why: 0.8 ATR. The swing high minus the hold low, divided by the ATR of 3.00, gives 0.8. The card wants at least 1 ATR, so this is a drift along the line, not a pullback to it.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the dip in ATR. Under one, there was nothing to pull back from.
questions.simple: The dip is 0.8 ATR, which is under the 1 ATR the card needs, so it is not a pullback.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c03)
computed key on a proposed 1 ATR number
tied to held decision D-029

questions.q: Fill 48.60. The hold candle's low is 47.45 and the stop sits three cents under it. Stop distance below the fill, in percent, to 2 decimals?
questions.why: 2.43%. The stop is three cents under the 47.45 low. Divide the gap from the fill by the fill, 48.60, and multiply by 100. That is inside the about 3% a stop usually stays within.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop sits about 2.43% below the fill: a few cents under the low, divided by the fill.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook F62 and A13

questions.q: Account 40,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 95.90, stop 93.85. Shares from the risk math, rounded down?
questions.why: 97. Risk is 0.5% of the 40,000 account. Divide that dollar risk by the stop distance, the fill minus the stop. Round the result down to 97. The size is the smaller of this and the position cap.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. You never pick a size and back-fit a stop.
questions.simple: We can buy 97 shares: 0.5% of the account is the risk, divided by the stop distance, rounded down.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook A5
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Buy the open?
choices: No; over 4% past the trigger
No; a gap up voids the hold
Yes; the gap shows strength
Yes; the stop caps the risk anyway

Remove it; the trade is free

questions.q: Two six-day pullbacks to the 20 EMA. Which one does Brian Shannon prefer?

The heavy one; buyers will show
Equal; the touch is the touch

A 20 EMA pullback with a shakeout
A Remount of the 50-day line
A buyable dip; it closed back up

The buy order's trigger
An invalidation of the hold
The line the stop sits at

questions.q: Which name fits?

20 EMA pullback; old uptrend
Remount; the 50-day was lost
Bull flag; a pause in a run

A 20 EMA pullback, then a bounce
An undercut and rally of a line
An EMA Crossback; the first retest

The 20 EMA pullback setup
A Remount of the lost line
No trade; any break kills it

No; the close back up erased the loss
Yes; re-buy at 546.88 and hold
Yes; a stop-out means a bad setup
questions.answer: No; the stop did its job here

wrong.Yes; a stop-out means a bad setup: A stop-out does not make a setup bad. Judge the trade by the plan, not by what the stock does next. The stop is the exit, and taking it is the plan.
wrong.No; the close back up erased the loss: The stop fired when the low traded through 540.97. A later close above it does not undo the exit.

Yes; it is nearly at the 5R line

Held; the stop is at breakeven
Added to, buying the dip
Held to a fixed 8R target

Keep the close stop; resize for 4%
A real 1.5% stop; keep the size

wrong.A real 1.5% stop; keep the size: The stop comes from the chart, not from the size you want. Stop first, then the size from it, or skip the trade.

questions.q: Take the trigger?

Yes; any dip under the line is fine
No; any dip under the line is off
